title: Hierarchical heterostructure of SnO2 confined on CuS nanosheets for efficient electrocatalytic CO2 reduction†
abstract: The direct electroreduction of CO2 to ratio-tunable syngas (CO + H2) is an appealing solution to provide important feedstocks for many industrial processes. However, low-cost, Earth-abundant yet efficient and stable electrocatalysts for composition-adjustable syngas have still not been realized for practical applications. Herein, new hierarchical 0D/2D heterostructures of SnO2 nanoparticles (NPs) confined on CuS nanosheets (NSs) were designed to enable CO2 electroreduction to a wide-range syngas (CO/H2: 0.11–3.86) with high faradaic efficiency (>85%), remarkable turnover frequency (96.12 h) and excellent durability (over 24 h). Detailed experimental characterization studies together with theoretical calculations manifest that the ascendant catalytic performance is not only attributed to the heterostructure of ultrasmall SnO2 NPs homogeneously confined on ultrathin CuS NSs, which endows the maximum exposure of active sites and faster charge transfer, but is also accounted by the strong interaction between welldefined SnO2 and CuS interfaces, which modulated reaction free-energies of reaction intermediates and hence improved the activity of CO2 electroreduction to highly ratio-tunable syngas. This work provides a better understanding and a new strategy for intermediate regulation by interface engineering of hereostructures for CO2 reduction and beyond.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
One of the most promising approaches towards offering carbon-neutral energy is the electrochemical conversion of CO2 into energy-dense carbon compounds (e.g., ethanol and propanol) by increasingly abundant and low-cost renewable electricity.1–5 However, the direct electrosynthesis of multicarbon products has faced several challenges, such as low activity, limited product selectivity and the subsequent energydissipated product separation.4,6,7 In contrast, the electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2RR) and H2O to syngas (the simple mixture of CO and H2) represents more immediate
opportunities for industrialization because syngas is a critical C1 feedstock for producing methanol and other synthetic liquid fuels via the established industrial processes,4,8–12 such as the well-known Fischer–Tropsch chemistry.13 And syngas with a tunable CO/H2 ratio can be directly integrated with existing downstream chemical infrastructures by adjusting variable reactor conditions for various products,6,8–10,14 which potentially reduces the dependence on conventional fossil fuels and simultaneously mitigates atmospheric pollution.9 Toward this end, a suitable and efficient catalyst is highly required.
Previous research on the electrochemical reduction of aqueous CO2 to syngas mainly focused on noble metals and their composites,10 such as Ag, Au, Pd nanoparticles (NPs),7,15–17 Ag/g-C3N4, 18 Co/Au9 and Cu/Au nanostructures,6 which were usually synthesized by either electrochemical techniques9 or surfactant-guided wet-chemistry.17 Besides, a few cases of non-precious metal-based catalysts were also reported, such as Cu/Ni(OH)2 nanosheets (NSs),
19 pulsed-bias technique-treated polycrystalline Cu foil,20 CdSxSe1−x (x: 0–1) nanorods from a solvothermal procedure,21 Co3O4-CDots-C3N4 integrated composite,8 Cu/In2O3 core/shell NPs,

Moreover, catalysts synthesized by electrodeposition are limited by the size of electrodes and affected by the nonuniform substrate and impurity of the electrolyte, which is not favorable for large-scale industrial production. Therefore, it is critically desirable to develop cost-effective, Earth-abundant, efficient and stable catalysts with a large current density for pure and highly ratio-tunable syngas through scalable methods for practical applications,9 which is a grand challenge.
Among tremendous CO2RR catalysts reported previously,32–38 cheap, less toxic and Earth-abundant copper/ tin-based catalysts have been largely constructed39–43 as alloys,44 bimetals45,46 and composites of different phases (i.e. Cu/Sn phase,47 CuOx/SnO2 phase 48–50 and Cu/SnO2 phase, 51,52 etc.) and structures (i.e. core–shell heterostructures51 etc.) with various compositions. These catalysts were purposely designed to achieve high selectivity and efficiency for CO2RR to CO or formate by suppressing the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and simultaneously stabilizing the reaction intermediates of CO2 reduction.
44,48,51,52 However, if the almost inevitable H2 evolution for Cu/Sn-based catalysts could be utilized, the energy conversion efficiencies would be largely enhanced since H2 is one of the important constituents of syngas.
11 On the other hand, different from individual components, interfacial effects between multiple components with different heterostructures have significant influences on many heterogeneous catalysis reactions with enhanced activity because the electronic interaction at interfaces can modify the active sites and stabilize the key reaction intermediates.39,53–56 However, studies regarding interface engineering for intermediate modulation through interfacial interaction are limited for CO2RR among Cu/Sn-based catalysts,
50,52,57 especially for CO2 electroreduction to syngas,29 and this is probably because most reports about the Cu/Sn-based catalysts for CO2RR are limited to the study of the composition (ratio of two elements) effect for the CO2RR. The interfaces, which are either fully mixed by two phases52 or internally covered by one phase,48,51 usually achieve high activity and selectivity for CO2RR to CO or formate over largely suppressed H2 evolution. Thus, through rationally designing the interface of the Cu/Sn-based heterostructure, it is possible to balance the relative activities of CO2RR and HER with both suitable active sites for CO2RR and HER, achieving satisfactory syngas production.
Herein, low-cost and Earth-abundant SnO2 NPs confined on ultrathin CuS NSs to construct novel hierarchical 0D/2D heterostructures were designed through a facile scalable onepot method under mild conditions, and could serve as an elec-
trocatalyst for CO2 reduction to highly ratio-tunable syngas (CO/H2: 0.11–3.86) with high efficiency (FE) (>85%), remarkable mass activity (48 A g−1 at −1.0 V), excellent TOF of syngas (96.12 h−1 at −1.0 V) as well as satisfactory durability (over 24 h), which are among the best reported values for electrocatalysts for syngas production. Benefiting from strong electronic interaction between SnO2 and CuS, which was confirmed by experimental characterization and theoretical calculations, the reaction intermediate were modulated to facilitate CO generation. Meanwhile, the remaining uncovered surface of SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs is favorable for the HER, leading to modulated syngas production as demonstrated by experiments and theoretical calculations. In addition, by simply changing the ratio of reactants, engineered SnO2–CuS interfaces could be attained for different syngas compositions. Of note, different from the enhanced CO2 electroreduction with a metal–oxide interface previously reported, this is the first case to explore metal oxide–sulfide interfaces for CO2 electroreduction to tunable syngas.

The one-pot facile synthesis process is illustrated in Scheme 1 and the proposed synthesis mechanism is described in detail in the ESI and products were thus obtained (Fig. S1†). X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (Fig. 1a) clearly demonstrated that the as-synthesized product is a composite of hexagonal-phase covellite CuS (PDF 78-0877) and tetragonal-phase rutile SnO2 (PDF 41-1455). The well-defined sharp diffraction peaks also demonstrated the excellent crystallinity of the as-synthesized products.
To examine the microstructure of the products, SEM and TEM were performed. The SEM images in Fig. 1b showed that many ultrasmall SnO2 NPs with a size of ca. 3–5 nm (circled by yellow ring) were well decorated on the surface of thin hexagonal CuS NSs with a lateral size ranging from ca. several hundred nanometers to one or more micrometers. The as-synthesized SnO2/CuS NSs could also form a stable dispersion in EtOH, exhibiting the Tyndall effect under laser illumination (inset of Fig. 1b). The low magnification TEM images also showed the attachment of small NPs on smooth ultrathin NSs (see Fig. S2a and b†). The thickness of CuS NSs characterized by atomic force microscopy (Fig. 1c) is ca. 4.8 nm, corresponding to three-unit cells of CuS as the lattice constant of the unit cell is about 1.6 nm according to PDF #78-0877 (Fig. S3a†). The humps of ca. 1.5–5 nm thickness in picture 1 and 2 of Fig. 1c indicate that ultrasmall SnO2 NPs were decorated on CuS NSs, which is consistent with the observation of SEM and TEM images. These hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs were further characterized by HRTEM and HAADF-STEM. As indicated in Fig. 1d, the interconnected crystalline SnO2 NPs with an interplanar lattice fringe spacing of 0.33 nm, corresponding to the d-spacing of the (110) plane of rutile SnO2

These scattered dots are distributed randomly to form several diffraction rings, which are assigned to the (110), (101) and (200) planes of rutile SnO2, agreeing well with the XRD pattern. Furthermore, the HAADF-STEM image and EDX mapping (Fig. 1e) also demonstrate that SnO2 NPs are well-dispersed on the CuS NSs. It should be noted that the surface of CuS NSs covered by SnO2 NPs is still partially exposed. The SEM-EDX analysis revealed that the Sn : Cu atomic ratio of SnO2/CuS NSs is 21.67 : 78.33 (Fig. S2c and d†), which was further confirmed by the ICP–AES result (21.28 : 78.72). Other characterization studies including FT-IR, UV-vis absorption and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy of the as-obtained hierarchical SnO2/CuS are also presented in the ESI (see Fig. S4 and S5†).
To probe the possible synergic effect of unique metal oxide–sulfide interfaces at the hierarchical microstructure of SnO2/CuS NSs on CO2RR behavior, similar to previous limited studies about the effect of metal–oxide interfaces on CO2 electroreduction,53 we fully investigated their CO2RR catalytic performance, together with pure SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs that were purposely synthesized for comparison (for details, see the Experimental section). As shown in Fig. S6,† ultrasmall SnO2 NPs of ca. 3–5 nm and thin CuS NSs of 50–200 nm were separately successfully obtained. Fig. 2a shows the results of linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) tests in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. Compared to SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs, the hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs exhibit higher activity from −0.6 to −1.2 V in CO2-saturated solution, suggesting the synergistic effect of SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs on the improved CO2RR electrocatalytic activities. Of note, the reduction peak at low overpotentials for
both SnO2 and SnO2/CuS catalysts shown in Fig. 2a corresponds to the reduction of SnO2 to SnO according to the literature,51 which could also been observed in other references.52
Subsequently potential-dependent chronoamperometry (Fig. S7†) was further performed to investigate the CO2RR activity of the as-synthesized SnO2/CuS NSs. According to the results of chronoamperometry and the corresponding gaseous and liquid product analysis (Fig. S8 and S9†), the as-calculated potential-dependent faradaic efficiencies (FEs) of product distribution of CO2RR for SnO2 NP, CuS NS and SnO2/CuS NS catalysts are clearly shown in Fig. 2b and c, from which we could see that the main electrolysis products for all catalysts are H2, CO and formate in the potential range from −0.4 to −1.0 V. It is noteworthy that the FE trends of HER and CO2RR are just opposite for all catalysts, where the FEH2 decreased from nearly 100% at −0.4 V to below 40% at −1.0 V while the FE for CO2RR (FECO + FEHCOOH) increased as the potential became negative. This phenomena is mainly due to the increasingly larger CO2*
− coverage at higher overpotentials.59 Of note, the increase of FE for CO2RR of SnO2/CuS NSs was more remarkable, indicating CO2RR is most preferable on SnO2/CuS NSs among the three catalysts. As for CO2RR, the trends of FECO and FEHCOOH were dependent on catalysts. For SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs, HCOOH became the main product of CO2RR as the potential was changed to be more negative, which is consistent with previous studies about SnO2 nanomaterials
60,61 and sulfur-modified copper catalysts.62,63 However, for SnO2/CuS NSs (Fig. 2d), the onset potential for CO production is −0.4 V (vs. RHE) and the FECO is improved significantly to be ca. 70% with the potential at −1.0 V. This improvement resembles the enhanced CO selectivity for the Cu–Sn bimetal,45 Cu/SnO2 core/shell51 and CuO/hollow SnO2 heterostructure reported previously,52 which comes from the synergetic effect of the in situ formed SnO2 NPs and ultrathin CuS NSs. However, different from those reported Cu/Sn-based catalysts with high CO or formate selectivity,44,49 the SnO2/CuS NSs exhibited relatively low, yet stable FEHCOOH and moderate potential-dependent FEH2 and FECO, which endows such unique hierarchical NSs to act as a potential catalyst for the important production of tunable syngas (CO + H2) as mentioned above.
To this end, we investigated the syngas composition (volume ratio of CO to H2) at different applied potentials for SnO2 NP, CuS NS and SnO2/CuS NS catalysts. As shown in Fig. 3a, the range of accessible syngas ratio (VCO/VH2) for SnO2/ CuS NSs is 0.11 to 3.86 when the potential decreases from −0.6 V to −1.0 V, which meets the requirements of most commercial industrial processes,6,9 such as thermochemical methanol synthesis (VCO/VH2 = 0.5) and hydroformylation (VCO/VH2 = 1), etc,
10,11 and more importantly, the desirable syngas composition generally used for Fischer–Tropsch reactions (0.5–1.67),13 methanation (0.33),9 fermentation and alcohol synthesis (0.5–1)64 can be effectively realized by tuning over a relatively narrow potential window (200 mV) (Fig. 3a and b), keeping attractive energy conversion efficiencies as the syngas composition is adjusted.9 Such a result from SnO2/CuS NSs is comparable to that from the Co-modified precious Au

This result further demonstrates that the selectivity of electroreduction of CO2 to CO was enhanced for the SnO2/CuS NS catalyst. Meanwhile, unlike SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs, for which the FE of syngas (FECO + FEH2) decreases quickly with increased potential due to the formation of formate at a high overpotential, the FE of syngas for SnO2/CuS NSs keeps stable and high (>85.7%) in a narrow range of potential for optimal syngas production (Fig. 3c), which is especially beneficial for high energy conversion efficiency. To further reveal the efficiency of the admirable syngas performances of SnO2/CuS NSs, partial current densities of CO, H2 and formate of the three catalysts at different potentials were investigated (Fig. 3d and Fig. S10†). As shown in Fig. 3d, the partial current density of CO ( jCO) for SnO2/CuS NSs begins at −0.4 V (vs. RHE), corresponding to an overpotential of 0.29 V (the equilibrium potential of CO2/CO is −0.11 V vs. RHE), which is ca. 100 mV smaller than that of SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs. The significant increase of jCO of SnO2/CuS NSs beginning at −0.6 V indicated that the CO2 reduction to CO is much enhanced on SnO2/CuS NSs. When potentials were set larger than −0.8 V, jCO approximately increased linearly with the potential for SnO2/CuS NSs, while the slope of the jCO curves decreased as the potential increased for both SnO2 NPs and CuS NS. This behavior is due to the fast CO generation rate at SnO2–CuS interfaces with excellent electron transfer during CO2RR, compared to the
pure SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs. In addition, the SnO2/CuS NSs give a partial CO current density of 15.24 mA cm−2 at −1.0 V, which is 5 and 7.5 times larger than that of SnO2 NPs (3.13 mA cm−2) and CuS NSs (2.0 mA cm−2), respectively. On the other hand, as shown in Fig. S10a,† the partial current density of H2 ( jH2) for SnO2/CuS NSs is similar to that for CuS NSs, but decreased to 4 mA cm−2 at −1.0 V, while the partial current density of formate ( jHCOOH) for SnO2/CuS NSs is the smallest and increases the slowest of all three catalysts over the whole potential range (Fig. S10b†). According to chronoamperometry (Fig. S7†) and LSV results (Fig. 2a), the SnO2/ CuS NSs exhibited the highest total current density at each applied potential. Together with the corresponding FEs and partial current densities of each catalyst, we could conclude that the HER was suppressed and the selectivity and activity of CO2RR were changed remarkably when SnO2 NPs were decorated on CuS NSs to create active sites at the interface. Therefore, tunable syngas of different CO/H2 ratios with a high FE was readily attained by such a SnO2/CuS NS catalyst.
Besides, the mass activity (current per unit mass of catalyst) and turnover frequency (TOF), which are independent of the surface area of the electrode (either real or geometrical) and reflect the intrinsic activity of catalysts,65,66 were also investigated (Table S1†). As shown in Fig. 4a, the mass activity for the syngas generation of SnO2/CuS NSs achieves 48 A g
−1 at −1.0 V, which is twice more than that of SnO2 NPs (21.4 A g
−1) and CuS NSs (22.5 A g−1). The TOF of syngas for SnO2/CuS NSs was calculated to be 96.12 h−1 at −1.0 V (Fig. 4b), surpassing most reported catalysts (including noble and non-noble metal-based materials) for syngas production, which indicates that, to the best of our knowledge, the SnO2/CuS catalyst is one of the best materials with an unusual wide tunable syngas composition and a high FE over a relative low potential range (Table S2†). Importantly, this synthesis approach is simple and free of expensive equipment and the raw materials are cheap, Earthabundant and particularly propitious to practical application.

Although the CO2 adsorption on hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs is slightly lower than that of pure CuS NSs due to the negative effect of SnO2 NPs, SnO2/CuS NSs showed a larger Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) specific surface area (SSA) compared to pure SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs (Fig. S11b†), which may be caused by the enlarged slit pores formed by the accumulation of SnO2/CuS NSs (for more details, see the ESI†). Moreover, EIS was also performed to probe the electron transfer kinetics on the electrode interface. The Nyquist plots showed that hierarchical SnO2/ CuS NSs exhibited a smaller charge transfer resistance (Rct) (41.7 Ω) than SnO2 NPs (184.1 Ω) and CuS NSs (72.7 Ω) during CO2RR (Fig. S12†), confirming faster charge transfer from the catalyst surface to the adsorbed CO2 on SnO2/CuS NSs, which would result in largely enhanced CO2RR activity.
All the above results indicate that the SnO2–CuS interfaces play a vital role for the electroreduction of CO2 to CO, such as the reported metal–metal oxide interfaces.48 Therefore, Raman and XPS studies were conducted to probe the interfacial interaction (Fig. S13, S14† and Fig. 5). As shown in Fig. S13a and b,† a distinct band at 474 cm−1 originating from the lattice S–S stretching of covellite,67 and the peaks at 358 and 572 cm−1 are for SnO2 NPs with a small grain size. 68 Of note, the peak at 472 cm−1 of the Eg vibration mode of SnO2 NPs was overlapped by the strong lattice S–S stretching peak (Fig. S13b†).67,68 In addition, the A1g vibration mode of SnO2 at 610 cm
−1 for SnO2/CuS NSs red shifted about 15 cm
−1 compared to the pure SnO2 NPs
69 (Fig. S13c†), implying the weakened force constant caused by the interaction between SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs (for more details, see the ESI†).
Then, the chemical states and electronic properties of the catalysts were investigated by XPS, which further substantiated the existence of interaction between SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs in SnO2/CuS NSs. As shown in Fig. 5a, both CuS NSs and SnO2/ CuS NSs exhibited typical Cu 2p peaks of covellite, which are assigned to Cu(I) species.70,71 The sharp peaks with a weak asymmetric tail are due to the kinetic energy losses in the reciprocity between photoelectrons and free hole carriers.70,71 It can be seen that the Cu 2p1/2 (951.8 eV) and Cu 2p3/2 (932.24 eV) peaks of CuS NSs slightly negatively shifted to 951.58 and 931.65 eV after being decorated with small SnO2 NPs, demonstrating the interaction between SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs again.52 Furthermore, the atomic ratio of Sn to Cu of SnO2/CuS NSs determined by XPS was 0.28, which is consistent with the value determined by EDS (0.27) (Table S3†). This interfacial interaction also could be clearly inferred from the peak shifts or valence band change in the Auger spectra of Cu LMM (L3M45M45) (Fig. 5c), valence band spectra (Fig. 5d), O 1s and S 2p spectra (Fig. 5e and f) of the samples. As shown in Fig. 5e, the O 1s spectra of pure SnO2 NPs can be fitted into two peaks, corresponding to the lattice oxygen and Sn–O bonds.69 When SnO2 NPs were confined on CuS NSs, the O 1s spectra can be deconvoluted into three peaks and the newly formed peak at 532.87 eV can be ascribed to S–O, for the peak at ca. 169 eV in the S 2p spectra of SnO2/CuS (NSs) (Fig. 5f) is assigned to S–O species.70 This newly formed S–O bond demonstrates the chemical coupling between SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs in the heterostructure72 and leads to positive shifts in binding energies for the Sn–O (0.35 eV) bond and lattice oxygen (0.48 eV). Meanwhile, as displayed in Fig. 5f, except that the peak at ca. 169 eV is assigned to S–O species,70 both the S 2p spectra of CuS NSs and SnO2/CuS NSs can be fitted to four types of S species, typical of covellite.70 For CuS NSs, the doublet at 162.29 eV and 163.49 eV is attributed to the disulfide bond (S–S) of S 2p3/2 and S 2p1/2, while the two peaks at 161.47 eV and 162.67 eV can be assigned to sulfide Cu–S of S 2p3/2 and S 2p1/2. 70 In addition, the double peaks at 163.2 eV and 164.4 eV are not completely clear and could be referred to as complexes containing elemental sulfur or Cu-deficient nonstoichiometric sulfides, which could also be partly intended as a “fitting effective” doublet.70 When decorating SnO2 NPs, all three doublets of SnO2/CuS NSs displayed an obvious negative shift about 0.36 to 0.45 eV and the peak for the S–O species was formed, clearly corroborating the strong electronic interaction

Based on the results of overall XPS studies, we can conclude that the enhanced electron transfer from SnO2 NPs to CuS NSs at the interfaces promotes to lower the binding energy of Cu 2p and S 2p and increase the binding energy of Sn 3d and O 1s. This charge transfer interaction at the SnO2–CuS interfaces resembles the strong-metal-support-interaction (SMSI) effect at metal–metal oxide interfaces that has been reported to play a crucial role in various heterogeneous catalytic processes.53 Thus, it is plausible to infer that the construction of the SnO2/CuS heterostructure would enable charge relocation at the SnO2–CuS interfaces and boost the activity and product selectivity of CO2RR. 73
Since the stability of catalysts is a key factor for their practical applications, we evaluate the CO2RR stability of SnO2/CuS NSs at −0.8 V in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (Fig. S15†). Over the entire 24 h continuous test, negligible decay in total geometric current density (∼12 mA cm−2) and FE for CO and H2 (∼40%) were observed (the gaseous product is analyzed by GC every 2 h), revealing that SnO2/CuS NSs are good stable electrocatalysts for syngas production. Besides, as shown in Fig. S16a,† the SnO2 species maintained well, while partial CuS was converted to Cu2O and CuO after electrocatalysis.49 In contrast, the morphology of nanosheets was largely preserved, though the overall atomic ratio of Cu/Sn was a little larger than that of the pristine sample after the stability test, possibly due to the slight solubility of SnO2 in aqueous KHCO3 (Fig. S16b and c†). In addition, the atomic ratio of Cu/S also increased from 1.05 to 1.46 (Fig. S2d and S16b†) after electrocatalysis due to the partial removal of surface sulfur during CO2RR,
74 and further XPS analysis indicated that Cu(I) species remained as the main phase of SnO2/CuS NSs after the stability test, though a small amount of Cu(II) oxides (Cu(II)/Cu(I): ∼9 at%) were found, indicated by the weak yet obvious shakeoff satellite peak at ca. 944 eV and broader tails at the higher binding energy side of the two 2p peaks (2p1/2 and 2p3/2). 44 The oxide species were caused by the oxidation while the surfaces were exposed to air and moisture under open circuit potential conditions after electrocatalysis44 (Fig. S16dI†). Meanwhile, Sn(IV) species were not apparently changed49 (Fig. S16dII†). Taken together, these results confirmed the considerable stability of SnO2/CuS NSs, which is beneficial for CO2RR in potential practical applications.
To further elucidate the influence of SnO2–CuS interfaces on the product selectivity, density functional theory (DFT) calculations of SnO2 NPs, CuS NSs and hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs were performed by employing the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model.75 Generally, CO2 electroreduction often initiates with a proton-coupled electron transfer process, then the C or O atom protonation would result in the generation of OCHO* or COOH* species, which are the intermediate to formate or CO, respectively.52 The free energy diagrams of CO2RR intermediates and the corresponding optimized geometric structures of various states for SnO2 (110) and CuS (001) surfaces were first calculated. As shown in Fig. 6a and b, the protonation of the C atom to OCHO* species (ΔG = +0.97 eV
for SnO2, +0.74 eV for CuS) is endothermic and energetically more advantageous than the protonation of O atom in CO2 to COOH* species (ΔG = +1.09 eV for SnO2, +0.84 eV for CuS) on both SnO2 (110) and CuS (001) surfaces, which would favor formate as the final product for CO2RR and is consistent with the experimental observations (Fig. 2b and c) and previous literature reports.60,62 While for the HER, the free energy of H adsorption on both SnO2 (110) and CuS (001) surfaces is the lowest endothermic (ΔG = +0.78 eV for SnO2, +0.65 eV for CuS), indicating that the HER is preferable over the CO2RR on SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs, which is also unanimous with the experimental results (Fig. 2b and c).
On the other side, to explore the SnO2–CuS interfacial effect on CO2RR performance, the SnO2–CuS interface was constructed by binding the Sn2O5 cluster onto the CuS (001) slab since the surface-supported small oxide clusters are effective to describe the catalytic activity of the complex and the predominantly exposed crystal plane was (001) on CuS NS according to the HRTEM result. As shown in Fig. 6c, in palpable contrast to individual SnO2 (110) and CuS (001) surfaces, the O atom in the CO2 molecule prefers to be protonated to form COOH* species with a remarkably reduced free energy of ΔG = 0.52 eV at the SnO2–CuS interfaces, which is significantly lower than that on SnO2 (110) and CuS (001) surfaces (ΔG = +1.09 and +0.84 eV, respectively). Meanwhile, the formation of COOH* species is energetically more beneficial than that of OCHO* species (ΔG = +0.81 eV) and H* species (ΔG = +0.64 eV) at SnO2–CuS interfaces. Therefore, CO2 electroreduction to CO was the most energetically favorable reaction pathway among the three competing processes at the SnO2– CuS interface. Combined with previous Raman and XPS analysis, we can conclude that the electronic interaction located at the as-built abundant SnO2–CuS interfaces can effectively enhance the activity of CO2RR over the HER and tune the selectivity of CO2 reduction to CO over formate. Taking previous morphology characterization studies together, it can be inferred that CO2 electroreduction to CO mainly occurred at the SnO2–CuS interfaces in hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs while the remaining non-contact surface of SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs mainly served as H2 evolution active sites. Consequently, highly ratio-tunable syngas can be effectively attained on hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs with tailored interfaces of balanced CO2RR to CO and HER processes, which is in good agreement with the obtained experimental results. According to the literature49,65,76 and above discussion of theoretical calculation and experiment results, the possible mechanism of CO2 reduction to CO is summarized and displayed in Fig. 6d. After the formation of adsorbed CO2* (* represents intermediate species adsorbed on the active site) on the interface of SnO2/ CuS NSs, the adsorbed CO2* will subsequently be reduced to form the SnO2/CuS NSs-CO2*
− intermediate by an electron. By combining with one H+, this intermediate readily forms the SnO2/CuS NSs-CO2H* intermediate and then converted to the SnO2/CuS NSs-CO* intermediate by coupling with the proton– electron transfer process. Finally, CO is released and generated (Fig. 6d).
Based on these experimental and theoretical results, it is reasonable to conclude that SnO2–CuS interfaces play vital roles in the catalytic performance for syngas production, and to better understand this catalytic system and evaluate the crucial role of the SnO2–CuS interface, we compared the hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs with other Cu–Sn based electrocatalysts and other low cost electrocatalysts of high CO selectivity in terms of electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) activity (Table S4†) on the one hand, and on the other hand, SnO2/CuS NSs of other ratios (e.g. 1 : 1 and 1 : 3) and the physical mixture of SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs (SnO2 NPs + CuS NSs) with a similar Sn/Cu ratio of SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2) were prepared for comparison in CO2RR (see the ESI† for details). From Table S4,† we could see that compared to other Cu–Sn based catalysts and some other low cost electrocalysts of high selectivity for CO2RR to CO in aqueous, the hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs exhibited suitable wide-range tunable FE of CO together with appropriate complementary H2 evolution over a narrow potential range, which is attributed to the rationally constructed SnO2–CuS interfaces and is favorble for highly ratio-tunable syngas production according to the literature.4,6,7,9
The morphology and composition of the as-prepared catalysts were fully characterized by TEM, SEM, XRD, EDS and XPS (Fig. 7, S17–S18 and Table S3†). The electrocatalytic performances of CO2RR were characterized by LSV and chronoamperometry. As shown in Fig. S19a,† SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2) exhibited the largest current density over −0.6 V to −1.0 V, indicating the highest CO2RR activity. According to the corresponding chronoamperometry results (Fig. S19b–d†), the as-calculated FEs of different products and CO/H2 ratio for various catalysts (Fig. S20†) clearly showed that CO was the main product of CO2RR for SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2), (1 : 3) and SnO2 NPs + CuS NSs, and their FECO increased with the potential shifted negatively except that the FECO of SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 3) reached the maximum at −0.9 V and declined at −1.0 V. While for SnO2/ CuS NSs (1 : 1), the activity of CO2RR is much less than that of the HER, and formate prevailed over CO, which resembles the activity of individual SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs. Among those catalysts, SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2) exhibit the highest FECO at −1.0 V (∼70%), which is 5.5, 3.3 and 1.6 times higher than that of SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 1) (12.6%), (1 : 3) (21.2%) and the physical mixture (44.5%). While for the CO/H2 ratio, SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2) also display the widest range for syngas production among those catalysts (Fig. S20 and Table S1†). Moreover, from corresponding partial current densities and FE of syngas (Fig. S21†), we could conclude that SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2) possess the highest activity for CO generation; SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 3) and the physical mixture come next and SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 1) is the last. Meanwhile, the values of mass activity and TOFs of syngas (Fig. S22†) also demonstrate that the SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2) are optimized for the production of syngas with high intrinsic activity. Further EIS determination (Fig. S23†) indicated that SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2) possess the fastest electron transfer kinetics for CO2RR among those catalysts. Based on TEM and SEM observation of those catalysts, the different CO2RR performance could be attributed to the microstructure of those catalysts. Compared to SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 2) with ultra-

Moreover, our synthesis method for the preparation of ultrathin hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs can be easily scaled up. To demonstrate the large-scale synthesis, we performed the reaction with 15 mmol of CuCl2 precursor and obtained ∼1.43 g of the sample in a single batch (Fig. S25a†). The subsequent physical characterization and electrochemical test (Fig. S25b–d†) indicated that the scale-up of the preparation method is successful and has no influence on lowering the catalytic performance of hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, we have successfully developed a facile one-pot strategy for the large-scale synthesis of Earth-abundant, nontoxic and hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs. Compared to SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs alone, the SnO2/CuS NSs performed well in CO2 electroreduction to wide-range tunable syngas over a narrow potential range with high efficiency, remarkable mass activity, excellent TOF of syngas and considerable long-term stability. The morphology and structure characterization in combination with DFT calculations suggested that the rationally tailored interfaces in SnO2/CuS NSs account for the superior syngas generation. Moreover, the syngas composition could also be easily tuned by modulating the ratio of reactants to construct SnO2/CuS NSs with a different size and morphology, or in other words SnO2–CuS interface density. All in all, given current advances in the synthesis of multi-dimensional hetero-
structures for catalysis, this work holds great promise for understanding the interfacial effects and designing more highperformance and cost-effective heterostructures with rationally tuned interfaces for CO2 electroreduction to syngas and beyond, which might shed light on the mitigation of anthropogenic excessive CO2 emission.

sections.heading: Chemicals
sections.text: Cupric chloride (CuCl2, 99.995%), sodium sulfide nonahydrate (Na2S·9H2O, 98%), tin(IV) chloride pentahydrate (SnCl4·5H2O, 99%) and potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99.99%) were all bought from Sigma-Aldrich. Formamide (CH3NO, 99.5%) was purchased from Titan Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Toray Carbon Paper (TGPH-60), carbon black (Vulcan XC-72) and anion exchange membrane (Nafion® 212, Ion Power) were purchased from He Sen Electric Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Unless otherwise mentioned, all chemicals were used as received without any further purification and Milli-Q water (Millipore, 18.2 MΩ cm−1) was used for all experiments.

sections.heading: Synthesis of Na4SnS4·14H2O
sections.text:
According to the literature,77 28.82 g (120 mmol) of Na2S·9H2O and 10.52 g (30 mmol) of SnCl4·5H2O were first dissolved in 80 mL and 20 mL of water with stirring, respectively. Then, the solution of SnCl4 was added dropwise to Na2S solution with vigorous stirring. After the addition, the mixture was kept still at 45 °C for 8 h in an oven and then poured into 450 mL of methanol and placed in an ice bath for 48 h. White small crystals of Na4SnS4·14H2O were then formed and filtered and washed with fresh cooled anhydrous methanol, and then dried under vacuum for 24 h. The product yield was ca. 69%, based on SnCl4·5H2O.
Synthesis of hierarchical SnO2/CuS NSs with different Sn/Cu ratios
For the 1 : 2 case (denoted as SnO2/CuS NSs unless otherwise specified), 295.6 mg of Na4SnS4·14H2O (0.5 mmol) was dissolved in 10 mL of formamide with stirring. Then, 134.4 mg (1.0 mmol) of CuCl2 was dissolved in 10 mL of H2O and added dropwise into the Na4SnS4 formamide solution with vigorous stirring, yielding a cloudy suspension. After stirring for 10 min, the mixture was stored in an oven at 60 °C for 48 h. After cooling down, dark green products were collected by centrifugation at 2000 rpm for 5 min and then washed with EtOH/ H2O (4 : 1) and absolute EtOH 3 times. Finally, the obtained dark green product (Fig. S1†) was dispersed in ethanol for further use. The yield of the obtained NSs was ca. 70% based on CuS. To obtain different Sn/Cu ratios, 67.2 mg of CuCl2 and 201.6 mg of CuCl2 were used for the Sn/Cu ratio of 1 : 1 and 1 : 3 (denoted as SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 1) and SnO2/CuS NSs (1 : 3), respectively) and the other conditions were the same.

sections.heading: Synthesis of SnO2 NPs and CuS NSs
sections.text: For SnO2 NPs, 0.5 mmol Na4SnS4·14H2O (∼295.6 mg) was first dissolved in 20 mL of H2O solution. After stirring for 10 min at room temperature (RT), the white cloudy solution was stored in an oven at 60 °C for 48 h. Then, the product was centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 10 min to be collected and washed with ethanol 3 times for further characterization. For CuS NSs, the synthesis procedure was the same as the synthesis of SnO2/ CuS NSs except that 480.36 mg of Na2S·9H2O (2 mmol) was used instead of Na4SnS4·14H2O, and the dark blue product was centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 5 min to be collected and then purified by using ethanol 3 times.

sections.heading: Characterization and instruments
sections.text: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the as-synthesized samples were collected on a desktop diffractometer (D2 PHASER, Bruker, Germany) using Cu-Kα (λ = 1.54184 Å) radiation operating at 30 kV and 10 mA. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM), STEM energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (HAADF-STEM-EDX) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were performed in the same was as referred to in previous literature.78 Fourier transform-infrared (FT-IR) spectra were recorded on a Thermo Nicolet Avatar 6700 FT-IR spectrometer from 400 to 4000 cm−1. The elemental ratio of Sn : Cu in SnO2/CuS NSs was determined by using both an inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometer 710-ES (ICP-AES, Varian Instruments) and SU8010 equipped with an energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector. Nitrogen and CO2 adsorption–desorption isotherms were obtained using a Micromeretics ASAP 2020 Physisorption Analyzer. Prior to the measurement, samples were degassed under vacuum for 12 h at 80 °C. Raman spectra were recorded on an inVia reflex confocal Raman microscopy system (RENISHAW InVia) with a 532 nm excitation laser and calibrated by the Raman band of a silicon wafer at 520.7 cm−1 as the reference. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) was performed in tapping mode in air on a Veeco DI NanoScope MultiMode VIII system. A silicon wafer with a thoroughly cleaned surface was used as the substrate and the image was flattened using NanoScope Analysis software (version 1.40). Catalysts after the stability tests for characterization were collected through peeling off from the basal electrode under sonication in ethanol.

sections.heading: Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
All the electrochemical experiments were performed in a threeelectrode system at 25 °C on a computer-controlled CHI-760E. A 1 × 3 cm2 carbon paper was used as the working electrode. One side and the middle part (1 × 1 cm2) of the carbon paper were masked with Kapton tape, leading to the other side of the carbon paper with an exposed surface area of 1 cm2 for catalyst loading. A leak-free KCl saturated Ag/AgCl electrode and a Pt plate electrode (1 × 1 cm2) were used as the reference counter
electrode, respectively. All potentials were 95% Ohmic iR drop corrected unless otherwise noted and converted to the RHE scale as follows, ERHE = EAg/AgCl(KCl sat.) + 0.197 V + 0.059 V × pH. Chronopotentiometry was carried out under the same experimental setup without iR drop compensation.
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 was conducted in a custom-designed gas-tight H-type cell (GaossUnion, Wuhan, Fig. S26†). Each of the two compartments contained 27 mL of the electrolyte (0.1 M KHCO3) with ca. 23 mL headspace and separated by an proton exchange membrane (Nafion® 212, Ion Power). Before the test, 8 mg of the catalyst and 8 mg of Vulcan XC-72 carbon were mixed and dispersed in a mixture of 1 mL of water, 1 mL of ethanol and 20 μL of Nafion solution (5 wt% in propanol) and bath sonicated over 30 min to get a homogeneous catalyst ink. Then, 100 μL of the catalyst ink was dropped on to the 1 × 1 cm2 carbon paper and naturally dried.
Before all electrochemical experiments, the electrolyte was pre-saturated with Ar (pH = 8.8) or CO2 (pH = 6.8) for at least 30 min. A gas flow rate with 20 s.c.c.m. was controlled by using a gas mass flow meter (S500, HORIBA) and kept continuously bubbling into the electrolyte to retain solution saturation. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves were obtained at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1 in an Ar or CO2-saturated electrolyte. The electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) was evaluated from the electrochemical double-layer capacitance (Cdl) which was determined from CV measured in a non-faradaic potential region (−0.225 V to −0.425 V vs. RHE) at different scan rates (5, 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100 mV s−1) in 0.1 M CO2 saturated KHCO3. Half of the double-layer charged current (i) difference between the positive and negative sweep is equal to the scan rate (ν), and Cdl based on i = ν × Cdl. Thus, the Cdl is then calculated by plotting the half of the current difference at −0.325 V as a function of v and the slope of the line is equal to Cdl. Nyquist plotting of electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed under the potential of −0.75 V versus RHE (CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3) with frequencies ranging from 1000 kHz to 0.1 Hz, and the amplitude of the applied voltage was 5 mV.

sections.heading: Theoretical calculations
sections.text:
Cambridge Sequential Total Energy Package, which is known as CASTEP,79 was used for the first principles calculations in the framework of DFT, including electronic and structural performances. To describe the electron–electron interaction,80 the exchange–correlation functional under the generalized gradient approximation (GGA)81 with norm-conserving pseudopotentials and Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE) functional was used. A 750 eV energy cutoff and a 7 × 7 × 1 k-point sampling set were tested to be converged. A 0.01 eV Å−1 force tolerance, 5.0 × 10−7 eV per atom energy tolerance and 5.0 × 10−4 Å maximum displacement were taken into account. 15 Å is set to the vacuum space along the z direction as it is enough to avoid interaction between the two neighboring images.
